text: The present case concerns alleged restrictions imposed by the authorities on the exercise of the applicants' freedom of peaceful assembly.
The present case concerns the alleged lack of domestic remedies in regard to restrictions on the applicants' freedom of peaceful assembly.
The applicants' names and other relevant details of the applications are set out in the Appendix to the judgment.
The Government were initially represented by Mr M. Galperin, former Representative of the Russian Federation to the European Court of Human Rights.
The Government were later represented by Mr M. Vinogradov, successor to Mr M. Galperin as Representative of the Russian Federation to the European Court of Human Rights.
The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.
On 5 October 2018 the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 notified the prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow of his intention to hold a picket (пикетирование) on 11 October 2018.
The picket notified by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 was planned to run from 12 noon to 3 p.m. on 11 October 2018.
The picket notified by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 was to take place in front of the State Duma (lower chamber of the Russian Parliament) building in central Moscow.
Twenty people were expected to attend the picket notified by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19.
The aim of the picket notified by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 was to protest against the increase in the State pension age recently voted by the State Duma.
On 5 October 2018 a deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow refused to approve the location chosen by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 for the picket.

The deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow indicated that the venue chosen by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 was unsuitable for public events because it would be impossible to meet safety requirements there.

The deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow indicated that holding a picket at the chosen venue might result in disruption to the functioning of public utilities, transport, social or communications services.

The deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow indicated that holding a picket at the chosen venue might result in obstruction of pedestrian traffic or a breach of the rights and interests of citizens not participating in the notified event.
The deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow proposed that the picket be held in Moscow's Lermontov Park, some 3 km from the State Duma building.
The applicant in Application No. 29356/19 challenged the deputy prefect's decision refusing to approve the location of the picket before the Taganskiy District Court of Moscow.

The applicant in Application No. 29356/19 submitted before the Taganskiy District Court of Moscow that the aim of the public event was to make the State Duma deputies aware of the inadmissibility of raising the State pension age.

The applicant in Application No. 29356/19 submitted before the Taganskiy District Court of Moscow that it was crucial to hold the event in front of the State Duma building, as the deputies were there daily.

The applicant in Application No. 29356/19 submitted before the Taganskiy District Court of Moscow that the pedestrian pavement in front of the State Duma building was large enough to allow the picket to take place without obstructing pedestrian traffic or access to the State Duma.
On 10 October 2018 the Taganskiy District Court of Moscow dismissed the applicant's complaint in Application No. 29356/19.
The Taganskiy District Court of Moscow held that pedestrian and vehicle traffic at Okhotnyy Ryad Street in Moscow, the location chosen by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19, is heavy.

The Taganskiy District Court of Moscow held that the deputy prefect's finding that the location at Okhotnyy Ryad Street in Moscow was unsuitable for public events was justified, as holding public events there might endanger the safety of participants and non-participants.
The Taganskiy District Court of Moscow held that the deputy prefect's decision met the requirements of section 8 of the Public Events Act.

The Taganskiy District Court of Moscow held that the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 had been given a written decision within the established time-limit indicating the reasons why it was impossible to hold the public event at the chosen location and time.

The Taganskiy District Court of Moscow held that the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 had not been deprived of an opportunity to enjoy his constitutional right to hold a public event by choosing another location, including the location proposed by the deputy prefect.

The Taganskiy District Court of Moscow held that the participants' right to express opinions during public events and voice demands on issues related to political, economic, social or cultural life had not been restricted.
The applicant in Application No. 29356/19 appealed against the Taganskiy District Court of Moscow's judgment of 10 October 2018.
The applicant in Application No. 29356/19 submitted on appeal that the authorities had no legal grounds for refusing to approve the picket.
On 11 October 2018 the Moscow City Court upheld the Taganskiy District Court of Moscow's judgment of 10 October 2018 on appeal in Application No. 29356/19.
The Moscow City Court held that the Taganskiy District Court of Moscow's finding that the authorities' decision was lawful and well-reasoned was correct and sufficiently reasoned.

The Moscow City Court noted that by a decision of 5 October 2018 the organiser of the public event in Application No. 29356/19 was informed of the reasons why it was not possible to hold the public event at the chosen location.

The Moscow City Court held that a regional public authority has competence under section 12 of the Public Events Act to make to the organiser of a public event a well-reasoned proposal to change its location.
The Moscow City Court held that the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 was not banned from holding a public event because he was offered an alternative location accessible to the public.

The Moscow City Court concluded that the contested decision by the deputy prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow was within its statutory powers, the procedure for adopting it was complied with, there were reasons for adopting the decision, and its content met the applicable statutory requirements.

On 25 January 2019 a judge of the Moscow City Court refused to refer a cassation appeal lodged by the applicant in Application No. 29356/19 with the Presidium of the Moscow City Court for examination.

The judge of the Moscow City Court who refused to refer the cassation appeal in Application No. 29356/19 referred to Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 when endorsing the reasoning of the lower courts.

On 17 April 2019 a judge of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation refused to refer the applicant's cassation appeal in Application No. 29356/19 for consideration by the Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation.

The judge of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation found that no significant violations of substantive or procedural law had influenced the outcome of the proceedings in Application No. 29356/19.
The applicants in Application No. 31119/19 are human rights activists.
On 10 December 2018 the applicants in Application No. 31119/19 notified the Moscow government of their intention to hold a public gathering on 22 December 2018 in Pushkin Square in central Moscow.
The public gathering notified by the applicants in Application No. 31119/19 was planned to run from 2 to 5 p.m. on 22 December 2018.
About 1,000 people were expected to attend the public gathering notified by the applicants in Application No. 31119/19.
The aim of the public gathering notified by the applicants in Application No. 31119/19 was to mark the anniversary of the first post-war political protest held in Pushkin Square on 5 December 1965.
The aim of the public gathering notified by the applicants in Application No. 31119/19 was to urge the authorities to respect rights to freedom of expression and assembly.
The applicants in Application No. 31119/19 promised not to disrupt traffic during the planned public gathering.

On 12 December 2018 the Moscow Department of Regional Security informed the applicants in Application No. 31119/19 that another public event was scheduled to take place in Pushkin Square on 22 December 2018.
The Moscow Department of Regional Security proposed that the applicants' gathering in Application No. 31119/19 be held at a special venue for public events in Sokolniki Park.
On 13 December 2018 three applicants in Application No. 31119/19 submitted to the Moscow government a written proposal for an agreement over the location of the public event.
Three applicants in Application No. 31119/19 pointed out the importance of holding the event in Pushkin Square, stemming from the fact that the protest of 5 December 1965 had also been held there.

Three applicants in Application No. 31119/19 stated that the alternative location proposed by the Moscow Department of Regional Security (Sokolniki Park) was incompatible with the event's purposes as it was too far away from the headquarters of the public authorities targeted by its intended message.

Three applicants in Application No. 31119/19 requested further information about the event planned in Pushkin Square on 22 December 2018, in particular its time frame and the contact details of its organisers.

Three applicants in Application No. 31119/19 asked that the Moscow government propose a time slot that would not overlap with the other event planned in Pushkin Square on 22 December 2018 and assist in negotiations with its organisers.
The applicants in Application No. 31119/19 did not receive a reply to their written proposal for an agreement over the location of the public event submitted on 13 December 2018.

On 13 December 2018 all applicants in Application No. 31119/19 challenged the refusal to approve the public gathering before the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow, on the grounds that it was not sufficiently reasoned.

The applicants in Application No. 31119/19 submitted before the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow that the Moscow government had not explained why it was not possible to hold the two events simultaneously in Pushkin Square.

The applicants in Application No. 31119/19 submitted before the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow that the Moscow government had not mentioned at what time the other event was planned and why it would be impossible to hold the applicants' event before or after it.
The applicants in Application No. 31119/19 stressed before the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow that Pushkin Square was the only venue that would allow the event's purposes to be achieved.

The applicants in Application No. 31119/19 relied before the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow on Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018, in particular its requirements that any interference by a public authority with the right to freedom of public assembly had to be lawful, necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim.

The applicants in Application No. 31119/19 relied before the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow on Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018, in particular its requirement that interference be justified through the submission of evidence of specific facts making it impossible to hold the public event at the chosen location or time.
On 20 December 2018 the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow dismissed the applicants' complaint in Application No. 31119/19.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow referred to Article 11 of the Convention, the applicable domestic provisions and Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 when dismissing the applicants' complaint in Application No. 31119/19.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that regional and local law-enforcement authorities have an obligation to ensure public order and safety during public events and should take these circumstances into account when proposing to change the location of a public event.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that the law-enforcement authorities complied with the statutory requirements when proposing to change the location of the applicants' public event in Application No. 31119/19.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that the Moscow government, when preparing its reply to the notification of the public event lodged on 11 December 2018, sent a request for information to the office of the prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow found that the office of the prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow replied that another event had already been planned to take place in Pushkin Square on 22 December 2018 from 7.30 a.m. to 8 p.m., namely the 'Moscow Traditions of New Year Celebrations'.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow found that the holding of the 'Moscow Traditions of New Year Celebrations' event in Pushkin Square on 22 December 2018 had been approved on 21 November 2018.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that the Moscow government complied with its obligation to submit to the court evidence of specific facts making it impossible to hold the public event at the chosen location and/or time.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that the law does not provide for any obligation to submit evidence of specific facts making it impossible to hold the public event to the organisers of public events.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that there was no reason to believe that it would be impossible to achieve the event's purposes if it were to be held at another location.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that the law-enforcement authorities complied with the statutory prohibition on putting public order and safety of citizens at risk if holding a public event at the same venue where a popular cultural event has already been approved.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that non-compliance by the applicants in Application No. 31119/19 with the statutory prohibition could amount to an abuse of the right to freedom of assembly, which falls outside of the scope of judicial protection.
On 20 December 2018 three applicants in Application No. 31119/19 appealed against the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow's judgment.

Three applicants in Application No. 31119/19 extensively relied on the European Court of Human Rights' findings in the case of Lashmankin and Others v. Russia (nos. 57818/09 and 14 others, 7 February 2017) in their appeal.
Three applicants in Application No. 31119/19 reiterated the arguments they had made before the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow in their appeal.
On 21 December 2018 the Moscow City Court upheld the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow's judgment in Application No. 31119/19.
The Moscow City Court endorsed the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow's reasoning in Application No. 31119/19, referring to Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018.

The Moscow City Court held that the appellants' arguments that the law-enforcement authorities had not considered the possibility of holding two events simultaneously did not warrant the quashing of the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow's judgment.

The Moscow City Court found that before sending a reply to the event organisers in Application No. 31119/19, the Moscow government had received information from the office of the prefect of the Central Administrative District of Moscow, the Moscow Department of Cultural Heritage and the Moscow Department of Commerce.

The Moscow City Court found that the celebrations in Pushkin Square on 22 December 2018 would occupy 3,000 sq. m, making it impossible to hold the applicants' public event in Application No. 31119/19.

The Moscow City Court concluded that the contested decision by the Moscow government in Application No. 31119/19 was within its statutory powers, the procedure for its adoption was respected, there were reasons for adopting that decision, and its content met the applicable statutory requirements.
On 25 December 2018 the other three applicants in Application No. 31119/19 lodged an appeal against the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow's judgment.
On 6 June 2019 the Moscow City Court dismissed the appeal lodged on 25 December 2018 by the other three applicants in Application No. 31119/19.
The parties in Application No. 31119/19 did not provide a copy of the Moscow City Court's judgment of 6 June 2019.
The applicants in Application No. 31119/19 lodged two separate cassation appeals.
On 18 June 2019 a judge of the Moscow City Court refused to refer one of the cassation appeals in Application No. 31119/19 to the Presidium of the Moscow City Court for examination.
On 29 August 2019 a judge of the Moscow City Court refused to refer the other cassation appeal in Application No. 31119/19 to the Presidium of the Moscow City Court for examination.
The parties in Application No. 31119/19 did not provide copies of the decisions refusing to refer the cassation appeals to the Presidium of the Moscow City Court.
On 15 August 2019 applicants in Application No. 31119/19 lodged a cassation appeal with the Presidium of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation.
On 24 September 2019 applicants in Application No. 31119/19 lodged a cassation appeal with the Presidium of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation.

The applicants in Application No. 31119/19 reiterated their previous arguments in their cassation appeals to the Presidium of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation, stressing that the domestic courts had failed to apply Article 11 of the Convention interpreted in the light of the European Court of Human Rights' case-law.

On 17 September 2019 a judge of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation refused to refer one of the applicants' cassation appeals in Application No. 31119/19 for consideration by the Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation.

On 22 November 2019 a judge of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation refused to refer the other applicants' cassation appeal in Application No. 31119/19 for consideration by the Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation.

The judge of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation found no significant violations of substantive or procedural law which had influenced the outcome of the proceedings in Application No. 31119/19.
The Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015) entered into force on 15 September 2015.

The Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015) replaced Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure governing the procedure for examining complaints about decisions, acts or omissions of State and municipal authorities and officials.

The Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015) replaced the Judicial Review Act (Law no. 4966-1 of 27 April 1993 on judicial review of decisions and acts violating citizens' rights and freedoms).

Under Article 219 § 4 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), a complaint against the authorities' decisions concerning the change of location or time of a public event must be lodged with a court within ten days of the date on which the complainant learnt of the breach of his rights.

Under Article 226 § 4 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), complaints against authorities' decisions concerning the change of location or time of a public event must be examined by courts within ten days.

Under Article 226 § 4 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), if a complaint is lodged before the planned date of the public event, it must be examined at the latest on the eve of that date.

Under Article 227 §§ 4 and 6 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), a reasoned judicial decision must be prepared as soon as possible on the same day and immediately served on the complainant.
Under Article 227 § 8 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), the judicial decision is subject to immediate enforcement.

Under Article 305 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), if an appeal has been lodged against the first-instance decision before the planned date of the public event, it must be examined at the latest on the eve of that date.
Under Article 226 § 8 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), when examining the case, the court must review the lawfulness of the contested decision.

Under Article 226 § 9 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), the court must examine whether the State or municipal authority had competence to make the contested decision, whether the procedure prescribed by law for its adoption was respected, whether the contested decision was taken on the grounds prescribed by law, and whether the contents of the contested decision met the requirements of law.
Under Article 226 § 11 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), the burden of proof as to the lawfulness of the contested decision lies with the authority concerned.

Under Article 226 § 11 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), the complainant has to prove that his rights and freedoms have been breached by the contested decision and that he has complied with the time-limit for lodging the complaint.

Under Article 227 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), the court allows the complaint if it has been established that the contested decision is unlawful and breaches the complainant's rights or freedoms, and in that case requires the authority to remedy the breach of the citizen's rights or to stop hindering such rights.

Under Article 227 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), when necessary, the court determines specific steps to be taken to remedy the violation and sets out the time-limit.

Under Article 318 §§ 1 and 2 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (Law no. 21-FZ of 8 March 2015), after unsuccessful recourse to the appeal court, the complainant can lodge a cassation appeal within six months from the delivery of the appeal decision.

Under Article 319 § 2.1 of the Code of Administrative Procedure as revised by Law no. 103-FZ of 5 April 2016, a cassation appeal should have been lodged with the presidium of the regional supreme court.

Under Article 319 § 2.3 of the Code of Administrative Procedure as in force at the time, a cassation appeal could subsequently be lodged with the Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation.

On 26 June 2018 the Plenary of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation adopted Ruling no. 28 'On certain questions arising during judicial examination of administrative cases and cases on administrative offences related to the application of the legislation on public events'.
section_path: B. Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 was adopted with a view to ensuring consistency in judicial practice and provided the judiciary with guidelines on the application of the Public Events Act when examining administrative complaints.
section_path: B. Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 is summarised in Kablis v. Russia (nos. 48310/16 and 59663/17, §§ 29-33, 30 April 2019).
section_path: B. Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that a refusal to approve a public event, its location or time or the manner in which it is to be conducted may be challenged before a court either by the event organiser or by a person appointed by the organiser to fulfil certain organisational tasks (point 2).
section_path: B. Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that when examining administrative complaints about public events, courts have to examine whether the interference by a public authority with the right to freedom of public assembly was lawful, necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim (point 9).
section_path: B. Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that courts must examine all the grounds advanced by the public authority and all the evidence submitted by it and assess whether the reasons for the interference were relevant and sufficient (point 9).
section_path: B. Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that a proposal to change the location or time of a public event or the manner in which it is to be conducted must not be arbitrary or unreasoned, and must mention specific facts showing that public interest considerations make it manifestly impossible to hold the public event at the chosen location or time (point 12).
section_path: B. Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that public interests justifying a change of location or time may include normal functioning of essential public utilities, social and transport infrastructure and communications; maintenance of public order and safety of citizens; disruption of pedestrians or traffic or of citizens' access to residential premises or to social or transport facilities; and other similar considerations (point 12).
section_path: B. Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that inconvenience caused to citizens by a public event or an assumption by the authorities that there might be a risk of such inconvenience may not in themselves be considered valid reasons for changing the location or time of a public event (point 12).
section_path: B. Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that the public authority must submit to the court evidence of specific facts making it impossible to hold the public event at the chosen location or time, and courts may not take into account any circumstances which were not mentioned in the proposal to change the location or time of the public event (point 12).
section_path: B. Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that the public authority must suggest a specific alternative location and time for the public event compatible with its purposes and its social and political significance (point 13).
section_path: B. Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that the organiser must reply in writing, stating whether he or she accepts the proposed alternative location and/or time, no later than three days before the planned date of the event, and may also propose another location or time for approval (point 13).
section_path: B. Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that if the organiser wants to change the date of the event, he must submit a new notification (point 13).
section_path: B. Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: The Government submitted seventeen judgments delivered by domestic courts between July 2018 and November 2019, with references to Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018, and sometimes Article 11 of the Convention and the European Court of Human Rights' relevant case-law.
section_path: C. Domestic practice on the application of Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: In most of the seventeen judgments submitted by the Government, first-instance courts found local authorities' refusals to approve public events unjustified due to insufficient evidence regarding the unsuitability of the selected location or timing.
section_path: C. Domestic practice on the application of Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: In most of the seventeen judgments submitted by the Government, first-instance courts found local authorities' refusals to approve public events unjustified due to insufficient evidence regarding the inability to hold two events simultaneously for security reasons.
section_path: C. Domestic practice on the application of Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: In the seventeen judgments submitted by the Government, courts deemed any refusal unjustified where the authorities failed to propose an alternative location or time for the public event.
section_path: C. Domestic practice on the application of Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: In the seventeen judgments submitted by the Government, courts deemed any refusal unjustified where the authorities' suggestions for alternative locations did not align with the organisers' intended message of the event.
section_path: C. Domestic practice on the application of Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: In cases where the authorities' refusals to approve the location and time of the public event were found to be lawful and well-reasoned, first-instance courts scrutinized the reasons behind these decisions, including assessment of potential participant numbers making it impossible to host two events concurrently at one place.
section_path: C. Domestic practice on the application of Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: In cases where the authorities' refusals to approve the location and time of the public event were found to be lawful and well-reasoned, first-instance courts scrutinized the reasons behind these decisions, including consideration of construction works planned at the chosen location and time of the event.
section_path: C. Domestic practice on the application of Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: In some instances, appellate courts overturned lower courts' decisions, finding that local authorities' refusals to approve public events were not well-reasoned because they lacked reference to specific facts or evidence.
section_path: C. Domestic practice on the application of Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018

text: The Supreme Court of the Russian Federation ruled in several cases that local authorities' refusals to approve public events were unlawful or ill-founded, overturning lower courts' decisions and either ordering re-examination of the case or issuing a new decision.

text: The Venice Commission issued a document entitled 'The Compilation of Venice Commission Opinions Concerning Freedom of Assembly' on 1 July 2014 (CDL-PI(2014)0003).
section_path: 1. The European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: The Venice Commission's Compilation of Opinions Concerning Freedom of Assembly (CDL-PI(2014)0003) states that location is one of the key aspects of freedom of assembly and that the privilege of the organiser to decide which location fits best for the purpose of the assembly is part of the very essence of freedom of assembly.
section_path: 1. The European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: The Venice Commission's Compilation of Opinions Concerning Freedom of Assembly (CDL-PI(2014)0003) states that assemblies in public spaces should not have to give way to more routine uses of the space, as use of public space for an assembly is just as much a legitimate use as any other.
section_path: 1. The European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: The Venice Commission's Compilation of Opinions Concerning Freedom of Assembly (CDL-PI(2014)0003) states that the purpose of an assembly is often closely linked to a certain location and freedom of assembly includes the right of the assembly to take place within 'sight and sound' of its target object.
section_path: 1. The European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: The Venice Commission's Compilation of Opinions Concerning Freedom of Assembly (CDL-PI(2014)0003) states that proper restrictions on the use of public places are based on whether the assembly will actually interfere with or disrupt the designated use of a location, and that the mere possibility of an assembly causing inconvenience does not provide a justification for prohibiting it.
section_path: 1. The European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: The Venice Commission's Compilation of Opinions Concerning Freedom of Assembly (CDL-PI(2014)0003) stresses that it is the privilege of the organiser to decide which location fits best, as demonstrations often need to be conducted in certain specific areas in order to attract attention, and that respect for the autonomy of the organizer in deciding on the place of the event should be the norm.
section_path: 1. The European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: The Venice Commission's Compilation of Opinions Concerning Freedom of Assembly (CDL-PI(2014)0003) states that the State has a duty to facilitate and protect peaceful assembly.
section_path: 1. The European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: The Venice Commission's Compilation of Opinions Concerning Freedom of Assembly (CDL-PI(2014)0003) recommends that a co-operative process between the organizer and the authority be established in order to give the organizer the possibility to improve the framework of the assembly, and that the decision-making and review process be fair and transparent.
section_path: 1. The European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: The Venice Commission's Compilation of Opinions Concerning Freedom of Assembly (CDL-PI(2014)0003) states that the organizer of an assembly should not be compelled or coerced either to accept whatever alternative(s) the authorities propose or to negotiate with the authorities about key aspects, particularly the time or place, of a planned assembly, as to require otherwise would undermine the very essence of the right to freedom of peaceful assembly.
section_path: 1. The European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: The implementation of the judgment in Lashmankin and Others v. Russia and seventy-two other repetitive cases fell under the enhanced supervision procedure of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe.

At its 1377bis (Human Rights) meeting from 1 to 3 September 2020, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe examined the status of execution in the Lashmankin group of cases and adopted decision CM/Del/Dec(2020)1377bis/H46-33.

The Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe noted in decision CM/Del/Dec(2020)1377bis/H46-33 that although certain positive steps were taken in the Lashmankin group, these were insufficient to attest to tangible progress.

The Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe welcomed Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 which provided important clarifications in respect of the relevant practice in the Lashmankin group.

The Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe noted the positive examples provided by the Russian authorities in their action plan, consisting of twenty judicial decisions delivered by courts of all levels between July 2018 and February 2020 in various Russian regions.
The Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe examined the Lashmankin group at its 1406th (Human Rights) meeting from 7 to 9 June 2021 and adopted decision CM/Del/Dec(2021)1406/H46-29.
The Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe welcomed Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 and other domestic measures in decision CM/Del/Dec(2021)1406/H46-29.

According to the Russian authorities' action plan submitted in connection with the Lashmankin group, in 2020 the first-instance courts found the authorities' refusals to approve the location, time or manner of conducting public events unlawful in 312 cases out of 815 similar challenges.

The Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe recalled in decision CM/Del/Dec(2021)1406/H46-29 the necessity of further changes to the Public Events Act with a view to introducing proper notification rules narrowing down the local authorities' discretion in authorising public events and obliging the authorities to assess thoroughly the proportionality of their decisions.
The Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe exhorted the Russian authorities to complete the work of amending the Public Events Act without further delay.
At the 1459th (Human Rights) meeting on 9 March 2023, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe adopted decision CM/Del/Dec(2023)1459/H46-21.

In decision CM/Del/Dec(2023)1459/H46-21, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe emphasised that the Russian Federation, despite having ceased to be a member of the Council of Europe as of 16 March 2022, was still obliged to implement the judgments of the European Court of Human Rights.

In decision CM/Del/Dec(2023)1459/H46-21, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe urged the Russian authorities to improve the notification rules on public events and to limit the discretion of local authorities in authorising public events.

In his Report of 21 May 2012 (A/HRC/20/27), the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association stressed that States have a negative obligation not to unduly interfere with the right to peaceful assembly (§ 39 of the Report).

The United Nations Special Rapporteur on the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association stated in his Report of 21 May 2012 (A/HRC/20/27) that any restrictions imposed on the right to peaceful assembly must be necessary and proportionate to the aim pursued.

The United Nations Special Rapporteur on the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association stated in his Report of 21 May 2012 (A/HRC/20/27) that assemblies must be facilitated within 'sight and sound' of their object and target audience.

The United Nations Special Rapporteur on the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association stated in his Report of 21 May 2012 (A/HRC/20/27) that organisers of peaceful assemblies should not be coerced to follow the authorities' suggestions if these would undermine the essence of their right to freedom of peaceful assembly (§ 40 of the Report).

The United Nations Special Rapporteur on the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association warned in his Report of 21 May 2012 (A/HRC/20/27) against the practice whereby authorities allow a demonstration to take place only in the outskirts of the city or in a specific square where its impact will be muted (§ 40 of the Report).

Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) were issued by the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) and the European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission) of the Council of Europe.

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that any restrictions imposed on assemblies must have a formal basis in law and be based on one or more legitimate grounds: national security, public safety, public order, the protection of public health or morals, and the protection of the rights and freedoms of others (paragraph 28).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that the legitimate grounds for restricting assemblies should not be supplemented by additional grounds in domestic legislation and should be narrowly interpreted by the authorities (paragraph 28).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that any restrictions on the right to freedom of peaceful assembly must be both necessary in a democratic society to achieve a legitimate aim, and proportionate to such aim, and that the least intrusive means of achieving a legitimate aim should always be given preference (paragraph 29).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that the principle of proportionality requires that authorities do not routinely impose restrictions which would fundamentally alter the character of an event, such as relocating assemblies to less central areas of a city (paragraph 29).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that banning or prohibiting an assembly should always be a measure of last resort and should only be considered when a less restrictive response would not achieve the aim (paragraph 29).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that any restrictions on assemblies should not be based on the content of the message that they seek to communicate, and restrictions must not be justified simply on the basis of the authorities' own disagreement with the merits of a particular protest (paragraph 30).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that people have the right in principle to choose the location or route of an assembly in publicly accessible places, including public parks, squares, streets, roads, avenues, sidewalks, pavement, footpaths, and open areas near public buildings and facilities (paragraph 61).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that assemblies should be regarded as an equally legitimate use of public space as other, more routine uses of such space, such as commercial activity or pedestrian and vehicular traffic (paragraph 62).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that where prior notification is submitted for two or more assemblies at the same place and time, simultaneous events should be facilitated where possible (paragraph 78).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that where simultaneous assemblies cannot be facilitated, the organisers should be encouraged to explore alternative options that might yield a mutually satisfactory resolution, and where such a resolution cannot be found, the authorities should still seek to accommodate the different assemblies ensuring that any alternative locations remain within sight and sound of the target audiences (paragraph 78).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that a 'first come, first served' rule must not be implemented in a way that enables some assembly organisers to 'block-book' particular locations, and that simply prohibiting an assembly in the same place and at the same time as an already notified or planned public assembly in cases where both can reasonably be accommodated is likely to amount to a disproportionate and possibly discriminatory response (paragraph 78).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that assemblies should be facilitated within 'sight and sound' of their target audience unless compelling reasons necessitate a change of venue, and that in those cases alternative sites should be provided that are as close as possible to the initially proposed site (paragraph 82).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that involvement in prior negotiations on the part of the organizers should be entirely voluntary, and an unwillingness or refusal to engage in dialogue with the authorities should not have negative repercussions for the organizers or their assembly (paragraph 124).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that those seeking to exercise the right to freedom of peaceful assembly should have recourse to a prompt and effective remedy against decisions disproportionately, arbitrarily or illegally restricting or prohibiting assemblies, and that the relevant court decisions should be issued prior to the planned events (paragraph 125).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that in both administrative and court proceedings, the burden of proof should be on the relevant state authority to prove that the restrictions imposed are justified, and that courts or tribunals should have the authority to review all circumstances of the case (paragraph 125).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that restrictions to the right to freedom of peaceful assembly must be both necessary to achieve a legitimate aim and proportionate to such aim, and that the reasons provided by the authorities for any restriction should be relevant and sufficient, convincing and compelling, and based on a comprehensive assessment of the relevant facts (paragraph 131).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that the principle of proportionality requires that authorities should generally not impose restrictions which would fundamentally alter the character of an event, such as relocating assemblies to less central areas of a city (paragraph 131).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that the types of restriction imposed on an assembly should in principle relate only to its 'time, place, and manner', not to the message that is being communicated, and that States enjoy a certain discretion in relation to time, place and manner restrictions (paragraph 145).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that at the core of the right to freedom of assembly is the ability of the assembly participants to choose the place where they can best communicate their message to their desired audience, and that it would be disproportionate if authorities categorically excluded places suitable and open to the public as sites for peaceful assemblies (paragraph 147).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that the fact that a message could also be expressed in another place is by itself insufficient reason to require an assembly to be held elsewhere, even if that location is within sight and sound of the target audience, and that other means of conveying expression such as placement of video screens are not adequate substitutes for the physical presence of assembly participants within sight and sound of the intended audience (paragraph 147).

The Joint Guidelines on freedom of peaceful assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017, third edition) state that the designated public authorities and law enforcement officials should make every effort to reach a mutual agreement with the organizers of an assembly on the time, place, and manner of the event (paragraph 169).
